newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-WORLD HOCKEY TREADING ON THIN ICE.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-WORLD HOCKEY TREADING ON THIN ICE.

text.p: From his private box at the ice hockey world championships life must have looked good to Rene Fasel.

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had just watched Canada skate away with the gold medal by beating Sweden 2-1 in front of another sell-out crowd at the new 14,000-seat Hartwall Arena to cap the most successful world championships ever.
Total attendance was a record 505,392, far surpassing the previous mark of 360,000, helping generate a profit of $23 million -- $10 million of which is destined for the IIHF coffers.

The championships also provided good advertisement for the sport ahead of the Nagano Olympics where ice hockey is expected to take centre stage with the world's top professional players taking part for the first time.
But as Fasel, who some insist has designs on the Olympic presidency, stepped onto the rink to present the medals there was concern the sport may be treading on thin ice.
Before Nagano, the IIHF will have to address several nagging issues, including drug-testing, roster deadlines, eligibility and officiating.
Aside from the Olympics, the IIHF has to steer the sport through a minefield of problems including the formation of a maverick super league.

Fasel's mood was soured the day before the final when he learned of a group of well-financed teams forming a renegade league to rival the IIHF-NHL-backed European Hockey League (EHL), which has just completed its inaugural season to mixed reviews.
Unhappy about the way the sport is heading, representatives from teams in Germany, Sweden and Finland announced the formation of a new NHL-style 16-team league to start in the 1998-99 season.
"I would say this whole situation is ridiculous," said Fasel, who will seek re-election in June for another four-year term as IIHF president. "Even stronger, I would say they are dreamers.
"This happened because some teams are frustrated because they are not playing in Europe. But we are prepared to fight and form our own permanent league. They have forced us into this situation.
"If they build a league of their own it will be a wild league and it won't be good for Europe. They are fighters but so are we. We are forced to go this way and will win for sure."
Currently the EHL format is based on soccer's European Champions' League.
But while European governing body UEFA possessed enough clout and money to fend off a breakaway circuit, the IIHF does not.
Like UEFA, the IIHF hoped to appease some dissenters by expanding.
But total prize money for the entire EHL last season amounted to one million Swiss francs ($700,000) -- about the same amount UEFA pays to each of its teams per game.

Another motivation behind the breakaway league is the many new arenas springing up across Europe looking for tenants. State-of-the-art facilities have already been built it Manchester, Oberhaussen, Helsinki and another is nearing completion in Koln.
"There is a lot of money to be made and a lot of people ready to grab it," said Rickard Fagerlund, president of the Swedish Ice Hockey Federation and a member of the IIHF council.
"These are entrepreneurs who are unconcerned about the total picture. What they're looking for is money.
"We are aware there are a lot of new arenas going up around Europe. All those arenas need events, so we understand what is happening, it's no surprise.
"But we think we are responsible for hockey in Europe so we have other ideas for the future that do not correspond to those ideas."
The IIHF has been forced to expand the world championships from 12 to 16 teams next year.
The move was made to ensure lucrative markets such as Germany, France and Italy remained in the A pool instead of being forced out by former Soviet satellites such as Latvia and Belarus.
Ice hockey is also struggling with the continuing chaos created by the Bosman ruling.
Top leagues such as the DEL (Deutsch Eishockey Liga) have begun to snap up much of Europe's top free-agent talent creating a drain on other leagues.

The German federation, meanwhile, claims the influx of imports has hampered the development of home grown talent and was partially responsible for the country's poor showing at the world championships where it came within a game of relegation to the B pool.
The exodus of players from Sweden and Finland has caused a sharp drop in attendance figures there.
So many players have left the Italian league that it is facing total collapse. Austria, France and Britain are struggling with similar problems.

The IIHF is also keeping a concerned eye on the state of the game in Russia where federation president Valentin Sych was gunned down in a gangland style hit just before the start of the championships.
Internationally, the IIHF is trying to bring all its federations in line ahead of Nagano.
But the Canadians are baulking at naming their roster on the August 1 deadline set by the IIHF. They want to wait until December 1 so it can name its best team.
Before the first puck is dropped the IIHF will also have to address the touchy issues of passports and citizenship.
In the past the IIHF has prevented players playing for an adopted country even when they have a passport.
"We will probably adopt more generous rules and players with passports for a country will be allowed to play for that country," Fasel said.
"There must be some changes before the Olympics -- or at least a more generous application of our rules."
